title: We Vetted 2000 AI Skills Before They Reached Developers — Lucas Palma, Nubank

primary.label: Security, Safety, Identity & Governance
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: Security & Defense
domains.rationale: The entire talk describes security operations: vulnerability management, supply chain risk analysis, skill vetting, and defense against credential leaks, destructive commands, and prompt-level confirmation gaps.

domains.label: Finance & Trading
domains.rationale: The implementation is at Nubank, a regulated bank. The talk emphasizes regulatory compliance, auditability, credential safety, and the extra constraints of operating in a financial environment.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: The talk centers on an internal developer marketplace and the CI/CD tooling (Skill Vector) that gates skill distribution for software builders within the organization.

summary: Lucas Palma, Information Security Manager III at Nubank, presents how his team built Skill Vector—an internal CI tool that vets AI skills before they reach developers through a regulated bank's internal marketplace. AI skills (bundles of instructions and context extending model or agent capabilities) look like configuration but behave like supply chain dependencies: when shared, the original author influences code generated by others, creating transitive risk. In Nubank's regulated financial environment, this raises auditability, credential-safety, and security-default concerns. Specific dangers include skills instructing AI to hardcode tokens (causing data leaks), use destructive shell commands, request excessive permissions, or introduce harmful typos. Skill Vector applies a hybrid scanning pipeline: deterministic regex-based checks for straightforward pattern risks, followed by LLM review for contextual behavioral risks the deterministic layer misses. Engineers can run checks locally during iteration, and scans repeat in CI after upload to verify the latest version. Findings are reported as PR comments for developer usability and emitted as SARIF for integration with the bank's vulnerability management program. Decisions range from allow to remediate to block, all before marketplace distribution. Over 2,000 skills scanned yielded 1,500-plus risks, with 1,000-plus remediated immediately and several blocked pre-distribution. A historical scan of pre-existing skills also fed risks into the vulnerability management program. A critical discovery was the prompt-level human-in-the-loop gap: instructions to "ask for confirmation" can be satisfied by the AI confirming with itself, creating a false sense of human oversight. The team now scans for explicit approval gates and hooks. Next steps extend the framework to plugins, MCP servers, rules, and hooks with adjusted risk profiles, plus tool-level enforcement, audit logs, and trusted gateways. Third-party skills must also be vetted—only cleared artifacts belong in the trusted marketplace.
whyItMatters: These concepts form a coherent security architecture for the AI agent era. The supply chain framing (AI skills as dependencies) is the conceptual foundation that motivates the entire pipeline; without it, skills would be dismissed as harmless configuration. The hybrid deterministic-plus-LLM scanning pipeline is the technical realization of that framing—deterministic checks provide reliability for known patterns while the LLM layer catches nuanced behavioral risks that regex cannot express. SARIF integration and PR-based feedback connect this new scanning capability to existing enterprise security operations (vulnerability management, CI/CD workflows), ensuring adoption in regulated environments rather than creating a parallel process. The human-in-the-loop confirmation gap is a critical AI-specific discovery that traditional supply chain security would never surface—it emerges precisely because AI skills contain natural-language instructions that an LLM can interpret and self-satisfy. Temperature-induced LLM inconsistency justifies why the deterministic layer is necessary and why the architecture is hybrid rather than LLM-only. The scan target taxonomy defines what the pipeline looks for, while local-to-CI dual scanning ensures coverage at every stage of the artifact lifecycle. Finally, the MCP server extension and tool-level enforcement concepts represent the forward path—applying the same supply-chain-security discipline to emerging AI infrastructure components (plugins, MCP servers, hooks) that were not part of the original skills scope, with runtime enforcement complementing static analysis. Together, these concepts describe a complete security lifecycle for AI artifacts: framing the risk, scanning at multiple stages, integrating with existing security operations, discovering AI-specific gaps, and extending to emerging infrastructure.
temporalContext: Video published July 29, 2026. The talk was delivered at a pivotal moment when AI skill security was being formally codified as an industry concern: OWASP published its Agentic Skills Top 10 (including AST02: Supply Chain Compromise) in June 2026, and NVIDIA released SkillSpector as open-source on August 17, 2026—approximately three weeks after this talk, making Skill Vector an early practitioner implementation of a pattern now gaining industry adoption. NSA/CISA published MCP security design guidance in June 2026. Empirical studies on MCP server vulnerabilities date to mid-2025 (VirusTotal analysis of 17,845 repos in June 2025; arXiv study of 1,899 MCP servers in June 2025). Nubank is confirmed as one of the world's largest digital banking platforms (135M customers, NYSE: NU since December 2021), operating in a regulated financial environment. Research as of August 23, 2026.
takeaways: AI skills behave as supply chain dependencies and must be vetted before entering any marketplace, just like libraries or containers
A hybrid approach—deterministic checks first, then LLM review for context—effectively covers both pattern-based and nuanced behavioral risks
Scanning should happen both locally during development and in CI after upload to ensure the most recent version is always checked
Prompt-level 'ask for confirmation' instructions can be satisfied by the AI confirming with itself; true human-in-the-loop requires explicit approval gates and hooks

concepts.name: AI Skills as Agent Capability Extensions
concepts.explanation: AI skills are defined as bundles of instructions and context that extend a model or agent's capabilities within an AI tool. When shared among engineers, the original author influences code generated by others, creating a unique transitive influence mechanism distinct from traditional code dependencies.
concepts.importance: Establishes what AI skills are and why they pose a novel risk category—configuration that effectively executes—requiring security treatment distinct from libraries or containers.

concepts.name: LLM-Based Behavioral Risk Review
concepts.explanation: An LLM is used as the second stage of the scanning pipeline to evaluate contextual behavioral risks that deterministic regex checks cannot catch—such as subtle prompt-level instructions, behavioral drift, and nuanced credential exfiltration patterns.
concepts.importance: Represents the application of LLMs as security analysis tools rather than code generation tools, a novel use case in the AI security space that complements traditional static analysis.

concepts.name: Human-in-the-Loop Confirmation Gap
concepts.explanation: A critical discovery that prompt-level instructions to 'ask for confirmation' can be satisfied by the AI confirming with itself, creating a false human-in-the-loop. True human oversight requires explicit approval gates and hooks that the AI cannot bypass autonomously.
concepts.importance: Reveals a fundamental security flaw in how human oversight is implemented in AI systems—confirmation instructions are not equivalent to genuine human confirmation.

concepts.name: Temperature-Induced LLM Inconsistency in Security Scanning
concepts.explanation: LLM-based checks vary with temperature settings, producing inconsistent results across runs. The hybrid deterministic-plus-LLM approach compensates: deterministic checks provide reliable pattern detection while the LLM provides contextual depth.
concepts.importance: Addresses a practical limitation of using LLMs for security analysis and justifies the hybrid architecture over LLM-only scanning.

concepts.name: MCP Server Security as Extension Target
concepts.explanation: The talk plans to extend the skill vetting framework to MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers, plugins, rules, and hooks with risk profiles adjusted per artifact type. MCP servers present new attack surfaces where tool metadata is read by the model as trusted instructions.
concepts.importance: Represents the forward-looking expansion of the vetting framework to emerging AI infrastructure components that introduce fundamentally new attack surfaces.

concepts.name: Prompt-Level Instruction Security Analysis
concepts.explanation: Scanning the natural-language instructions within AI skills for security risks—such as instructions to retrieve and hardcode tokens, use destructive shell commands, or request excessive permissions—treating prompt instructions as potentially executable code paths rather than documentation.
concepts.importance: Establishes that natural-language prompts in AI skills must be analyzed as executable instructions, bridging the gap between natural language and security-relevant code paths.

concepts.name: Tool-Level Enforcement and Approval Gates
concepts.explanation: Beyond pre-distribution scanning, the team plans tool-level enforcement with audit logs, trusted gateways, and explicit human approval hooks that the AI cannot self-satisfy, ensuring dangerous runtime actions require genuine human authorization.
concepts.importance: Adds runtime enforcement to complement pre-distribution static scanning, addressing the gap between static analysis and actual agent execution behavior.

concepts.name: AI Skill Supply Chain Security
concepts.explanation: AI skills—bundles of instructions extending model capabilities—behave like supply chain dependencies when shared among engineers. The original author influences code generated by others, creating transitive risk. This reframes configuration-like artifacts as security-critical dependencies requiring vetting before distribution.
concepts.importance: Foundational framing that justifies the entire Skill Vector pipeline. Without this lens, skills would be treated as harmless configuration rather than vetted dependencies.

concepts.name: Hybrid Deterministic-Plus-LLM Static Analysis Pipeline
concepts.explanation: A two-stage scanning architecture: deterministic regex-based checks first (fast, reliable, handles straightforward patterns like unsafe shell commands), then LLM-based review for contextual behavioral risks the deterministic layer misses. Both stages run locally during development and in CI after upload.
concepts.importance: This is the core technical architecture of Skill Vector and the primary engineering pattern the talk advocates. It compensates for LLM temperature-induced inconsistency by anchoring reliable pattern detection in the deterministic layer.

concepts.name: SARIF Integration for Vulnerability Management
concepts.explanation: Scan findings are emitted as SARIF (Static Analysis Results Interchange Format) to integrate with the bank's existing vulnerability management program, enabling compliance tracking and remediation workflows alongside traditional security findings.
concepts.importance: Bridges AI skill scanning into established enterprise security operations rather than creating a parallel process, critical for adoption in regulated environments.

concepts.name: PR-Based Security Feedback and Gating
concepts.explanation: Scan findings are delivered as PR comments for developer usability, with allow/remediate/block decisions gating whether a skill reaches the marketplace. This embeds security review into the developer's existing PR workflow.
concepts.importance: Ensures developer adoption by integrating into familiar workflows rather than imposing a separate security review process.

concepts.name: Internal Marketplace Artifact Gating
concepts.explanation: An internal marketplace where engineers discover and share AI skills, with a CI step (Skill Vector) inserted before distribution. Only vetted artifacts are allowed into the trusted marketplace, preventing unvetted skills from reaching developers.
concepts.importance: Centralizes skill distribution through a single vetted channel, preventing shadow distribution of unvetted artifacts.

concepts.name: Local-to-CI Dual Scanning
concepts.explanation: Skills are scanned both locally during development iteration and again in CI after upload, ensuring the latest version is always checked. This catches changes introduced between local testing and marketplace submission.
concepts.importance: Prevents false security confidence from local-only scanning; post-local changes might introduce new risks not caught by the initial local scan.

concepts.name: Historical Batch Scanning of Pre-Existing Artifacts
concepts.explanation: After deploying Skill Vector, the team ran a retrospective scan of all pre-existing skills already in the marketplace, feeding newly discovered risks into the vulnerability management program for retroactive remediation.
concepts.importance: Addresses the technical debt of skills created before the vetting pipeline existed, closing the security gap for the existing ecosystem rather than only gating new submissions.

concepts.name: Scan Target Taxonomy for AI Artifacts
concepts.explanation: Defined scan targets include unsafe instructions, behavioral drift, destructive shell commands, file modifications, credential requests, data exposure, overbroad permissions, and risky MCP usage—a taxonomy of risk categories specific to AI skill artifacts beyond traditional SAST categories.
concepts.importance: Provides a structured approach to what to scan for, going beyond traditional static analysis categories to include AI-specific behavioral and prompt-level risks.

sections.title: Introduction: making code safe at a bank
sections.summary: LP introduces himself as Nubank's product security manager with over a decade in financial services engineering. He frames the talk around protecting the developer workflow, not just generated code, as AI skills enter the picture.

sections.title: AI skills as a supply chain risk
sections.summary: Explains that the AI-era supply chain now includes skills, plugins, MCP servers, and agent rules alongside traditional packages and containers. AI skills look like configuration but behave like supply chain dependencies.

sections.title: What counts as an AI skill
sections.summary: Defines an AI skill as a bundle of instructions and context extending a model or agent's capabilities within an AI tool. When shared, the original author influences code generated by others, creating risk.

sections.title: The extra weight of a regulated environment
sections.summary: In a regulated bank, developers want faster coding and less repetitive work, but security teams must ensure auditability, credential safety, and security defaults. Specific dangers include hardcoded tokens causing data leaks, destructive shell commands, excessive permissions, and harmful typos.

sections.title: From plugins to a vetted marketplace
sections.summary: Nubank created an internal marketplace where engineers discover and share skills. A CI step—Skill Vector—was inserted before marketplace distribution to check whether each skill is safe and classify risks.

sections.title: What Skill Vector does
sections.summary: Skill Vector scans skills on creation and change, both locally during iteration and after upload. Findings are reported as PR comments and SARIF for integration with vulnerability management. Decisions range from allow to remediate to block, all before marketplace distribution.

sections.title: Deterministic checks, then the LLM
sections.summary: Outlines the hybrid pipeline: local scan, PR, deterministic scanner (regex-based for easy risks), then LLM review for context the deterministic checks miss. The hybrid approach compensates for LLM temperature-induced inconsistency. Lists scan targets: unsafe instructions, behavioral drift, destructive shell commands, file modifications, credential requests, data exposure, overbroad permissions, and risky MCP usage.

sections.title: Scanning over two thousand skills
sections.summary: Over 2,000 skills scanned yielded 1,500-plus risks. A single skill can carry many risks. 1,000-plus were remediated immediately, and several dangerous ones were blocked before marketplace distribution. A historical scan of pre-existing skills also identified risks routed into the vulnerability management program.

sections.title: What worked and what needed improvement
sections.summary: What worked: deterministic scanners for non-risk patterns, LLM review for behavior checking, SARIF output, and PR comments. What needed work: treating all comments equally, weak signals lacking context, unclear remediation guidance, warnings only harmless locally, and proactively detecting new marketplaces.

sections.title: Approval gates and human confirmation
sections.summary: Discovers that prompt-level 'ask for confirmation' can be satisfied by the AI confirming with itself, creating a false human-in-the-loop. The team now scans for proper approval gates, hooks, and tool execution paths. Treats skills like supply chain: review before upload, enforce local and CI checks, enforce on dangerous actions.

sections.title: Next steps and policies
sections.summary: Plans to extend the framework to plugins, MCP servers, rules, and hooks with different risk profiles. Tool-level enforcement, audit logs, and trusted gateways are planned. Third-party skills must also be uploaded and vetted. The goal is a trusted AI marketplace where only scanned, safe artifacts are shared.

organization.name: Nubank
organization.summary: Nubank (NYSE: NU) is one of the world's largest digital financial services platforms, serving 135 million customers across Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia. Founded in 2013 by David Vélez, Cristina Junqueira, and Edward Wible and headquartered in São Paulo, Brazil, Nubank leverages proprietary technology and data to build innovative financial products. Publicly traded since December 2021 on the New York Stock Exchange (IPO raising US$2.3 billion), the company has approximately 8,000-9,000 employees. Within its Information Technology & Security unit sits the Product Security & Assurance organization, including Application Security (SAST/DAST/SCA), AI Security (LLM applications, autonomous agents, AI infrastructure), Blockchain Security, Red Team, Mobile Security, and Vulnerability Management teams. Speaker Lucas Palma (Information Security Manager III, LinkedIn bio: 'Enabling safer Products and AI @ Nubank') leads AI security initiatives including the Skill Vector tool described in the talk. Engineering uses Clojure, Python, and Go, actively adopts generative AI assistants like Devin, and runs cloud-native infrastructure with CI/CD pipelines and chaos engineering. Nubank acquired AI/ML company Olivia AI in November 2021, demonstrating strategic investment in AI/ML capabilities.
organization.status: Active. Nubank is publicly traded on NYSE (ticker: NU), continues operations as Latin America's largest private financial institution, and actively invests in AI for both customer-facing products (AI-powered credit models) and internal developer workflows (AI skills marketplace, generative AI assistants). The Product Security & AI Security organization continues to grow, with active recruitment for Lead Security Engineer (AI) and AppSec roles as of 2026.

technologies.label: AI Skill Security Scanning Pipeline
technologies.summary: Hybrid two-stage scanning architecture for AI skill security: deterministic regex-based checks first (fast, reliable, handles straightforward patterns like unsafe shell commands and hardcoded credentials), then LLM-based review for contextual behavioral risks the deterministic layer misses (behavioral drift, subtle prompt-level instructions, credential exfiltration patterns). The pipeline runs locally during development iteration and again in CI after upload to verify the latest version. Findings are reported as PR comments for developer usability and emitted as SARIF for vulnerability management integration. Decisions range from allow to remediate to block, all before marketplace distribution. The hybrid approach compensates for LLM temperature-induced inconsistency by anchoring reliable pattern detection in the deterministic layer. Over 2,000 skills scanned at Nubank yielded 1,500+ risks, 1,000+ remediated, and several blocked pre-distribution.
technologies.role: Central technology: Skill Vector is the primary subject of the talk, presented as Nubank's solution for vetting AI skills before they reach developers through the internal marketplace in a regulated financial environment

technologies.label: SARIF Integration for Vulnerability Management
technologies.summary: SARIF (Static Analysis Results Interchange Format) is an OASIS Standard (v2.1.0, March 2020) defining a standard format for the output of static analysis tools. It enables developers to aggregate results from multiple tools and quickly identify problems. In the context of this video, Skill Vector emits SARIF to integrate AI skill scan findings into Nubank's existing vulnerability management program, bridging new AI-specific scanning capabilities into established enterprise security operations rather than creating a parallel process. The same pattern is confirmed across NVIDIA SkillSpector (SARIF 2.1.0 output via Pydantic models), JFrog skill scanning, and skill-veil. SARIF v2.2 is under active development by the OASIS SARIF TC as of early 2026.
technologies.role: Integration bridge: SARIF connects Skill Vector's scanning output to the bank's existing vulnerability management program, enabling compliance tracking and remediation workflows alongside traditional security findings in a regulated financial environment

technologies.label: AI Skill Supply Chain Security Framework
technologies.summary: The OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 project (published June 2026) validates the talk's central thesis that AI skills are supply chain risks. AST02 (Supply Chain Compromise, Critical severity) documents that skill registries lack provenance controls, configuration files have become active execution paths, and compromised skills gain the agent's full credential set. It lists real-world attacks including ClawHavoc (1,200+ malicious skills) and CVE-2025-59536. Recommended mitigations include internal skill mirrors/allowlists, automated CI/CD scanning gates, and change management for skill updates, directly mirroring Skill Vector's design. The SkillFortify academic paper (arXiv, 2026) formalizes the same threat model using Dolev-Yao attacker models, abstract interpretation, and capability-based security. This family establishes that the supply-chain-security framing the talk applies to AI skills is an emerging industry consensus, not a single-organization decision.
technologies.role: Conceptual framework: provides authoritative external validation that treating AI skills as supply chain dependencies is not just a Nubank-internal decision but an emerging industry consensus codified by OWASP and academic research

technologies.label: MCP Server Security
technologies.summary: The talk's planned next step is extending the Skill Vector vetting framework to MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers, plugins, rules, and hooks with risk profiles adjusted per artifact type. MCP introduces a fundamentally new attack surface where tool metadata is read by the model as trusted instructions, creating combined prompt injection, supply chain, and confused deputy risks. External validation is strong: OWASP published an MCP Security Cheat Sheet (June 2026), NSA/CISA published government cybersecurity guidance recommending SAST/SCA in pipelines and proactive scanning for unauthorized MCP servers (June 2026), VirusTotal found 1,408 likely malicious MCP servers out of 17,845 GitHub repos analyzed (June 2025), and an arXiv study of 1,899 MCP servers found 7.2% with general vulnerabilities and 5.5% with MCP-specific tool poisoning (June 2025). MCPScan (Ant Group) implements multi-stage MCP server scanning combining static taint analysis with dynamic LLM evaluation, demonstrating the feasibility of extending the same hybrid approach to MCP servers.
technologies.role: Forward-looking extension target: the talk identifies MCP server vetting as the next phase of the framework, planning to extend the same hybrid scanning approach to MCP servers, plugins, rules, and hooks with risk profiles adjusted per artifact type
